Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.

Item 1. Business

We design and sell high performance computing and adaptive computing products for data center, client, gaming, and embedded markets.

Item 1A. Risk Factors

Risk factor 1: We rely on third-party foundries and outsourced semiconductor assembly and test providers for a significant portion of our products. If any supplier has capacity constraints, yield issues, technology transition delays, quality problems, trade restriction exposure, cybersecurity incidents, or disruptions from natural disasters, our ability to deliver products to customers could be materially and adversely affected. We may not be able to secure alternate capacity on acceptable terms, and any transition could require qualification time, engineering resources, and customer approvals.

Risk factor 2: Demand for data center accelerators, server processors, client processors, gaming products, and embedded products can change rapidly because our customers manage inventory, capital spending, and product roadmaps based on their own end market expectations. A customer inventory correction, delayed platform launch, weaker macroeconomic conditions, or reduced cloud service provider spending could cause revenue volatility. If demand is lower than expected, we may hold excess inventory, incur cancellation charges, or record valuation adjustments.

Risk factor 3: Our business depends on the availability of advanced packaging, substrates, memory, power components, printed circuit boards, and logistics capacity. Shortages, allocation decisions, supplier consolidation, labor interruptions, geopolitical tensions, export controls, or shipping bottlenecks could limit our ability to meet customer commitments. Even when supply is available, increased input costs or expedited shipping costs could reduce margins if we are unable to pass those costs through to customers.

Risk factor 4: Competition in the semiconductor industry is intense and includes companies with greater financial resources, larger installed bases, extensive software ecosystems, and long-standing customer relationships. Competitors may introduce products with better performance, power efficiency, price, availability, or developer tooling. If our product roadmap, manufacturing execution, software enablement, or customer support does not meet market requirements, customers may delay adoption or choose competing solutions.

Risk factor 5: We depend on a limited number of large customers for a meaningful portion of revenue in certain periods. The loss, reduction, delay, or renegotiation of purchases by one or more significant customers could materially affect our operating results. Customer concentration can also increase forecast uncertainty because purchasing decisions may be influenced by product transitions, inventory management, capital budget timing, deployment schedules, and competitive benchmarking results outside our control.

Risk factor 6: Export controls, sanctions, customs rules, government procurement restrictions, and other trade regulations may restrict the sale, shipment, service, or support of certain products or technologies. Changes in laws or license requirements could reduce addressable markets, delay customer deployments, increase compliance costs, or require product modifications. Failure to comply with applicable trade restrictions could result in penalties, reputational harm, loss of export privileges, and operational disruption.

Risk factor 7: We must execute complex technology transitions, including new process nodes, chiplet designs, advanced packaging, firmware releases, and software stack updates. Execution delays, design defects, validation failures, or lower than expected manufacturing yields could reduce product availability or increase costs. Correcting defects may require redesigns, replacement programs, warranty costs, customer concessions, or delayed revenue recognition, any of which could adversely affect financial results.

Risk factor 8: Our products are incorporated into systems that may be used in critical infrastructure, enterprise computing, artificial intelligence, high performance computing, automotive, industrial, and communications applications. Security vulnerabilities, reliability issues, performance regressions, or interoperability problems could lead to customer claims, remediation costs, reputational damage, regulatory scrutiny, or reduced demand. We may also need to devote substantial engineering resources to firmware, driver, and software updates.

Risk factor 9: We make substantial investments in research and development before customer demand is certain. Long development cycles, changing standards, evolving workloads, and rapid technology shifts can make it difficult to forecast which products will generate sufficient returns. If we misjudge demand, product timing, pricing, or competitive positioning, we may not recover development costs, and our operating income and cash flows could be adversely affected.

Risk factor 10: Our intellectual property portfolio is important to our competitive position, but we may be unable to protect it fully. Third parties may claim that our products, designs, software, or manufacturing arrangements infringe their rights, and litigation can be expensive, distracting, and uncertain. Adverse outcomes could require damages, royalties, licensing restrictions, product changes, or limits on sales, while unsuccessful enforcement could weaken our ability to differentiate products.

Risk factor 11: Acquisitions, divestitures, strategic investments, and partnerships can create integration risks and execution demands. We may face challenges aligning systems, retaining employees, integrating product roadmaps, managing customer commitments, and achieving expected synergies. If integrations take longer than expected or do not deliver anticipated benefits, we could incur impairment charges, restructuring costs, operational disruption, or reduced management focus on core business priorities.

Risk factor 12: Our financial results are affected by currency movements, interest rates, tax rules, credit conditions, and global economic uncertainty. Higher borrowing costs, weaker customer demand, inflationary pressure, changes in tax law, or reduced access to capital markets could affect profitability and strategic flexibility. Because semiconductor cycles can turn quickly, unfavorable macroeconomic conditions may amplify inventory risk, pricing pressure, and demand variability across multiple product lines.

Risk factor 13: Climate change, water availability, energy reliability, and environmental regulations may affect our suppliers, operations, and customers. Semiconductor manufacturing can require substantial water, power, chemicals, and specialized facilities, and disruptions at supplier sites could affect our product supply. New environmental rules or customer sustainability requirements may increase reporting obligations, compliance costs, product design requirements, or supplier qualification work.

Risk factor 14: We depend on highly skilled employees and leaders in engineering, sales, operations, security, finance, and general management. Competition for semiconductor and artificial intelligence talent is intense. If we cannot attract, retain, motivate, and develop key personnel, or if workforce changes disrupt execution, our ability to deliver product roadmaps, support customers, and manage complex supplier relationships could be adversely affected.

Risk factor 15: Information technology systems, design tools, cloud services, supplier portals, and manufacturing interfaces are important to our operations. Cyberattacks, ransomware, unauthorized access, data loss, system outages, or vendor incidents could disrupt engineering work, supply planning, order fulfillment, financial reporting, or customer support. We may incur significant costs to investigate incidents, restore systems, notify affected parties, and improve controls.

Item 7. Management's Discussion and Analysis

Revenue performance reflected demand across data center, client, gaming, and embedded markets.
